newsitem.title: PERU: Computer problems blamed for Peru plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Computer problems blamed for Peru plane crash.

text.p: A Boeing 757-200 belonging to the Peruvian airline Aeroperu crashed off the Pacific Coast north of Lima early on Wednesday morning, killing all 70 passengers and crew on board.
The Peruvian government blamed computer problems aboard the plane for the accident, which claimed victims from 11 countries. Aeroperu cited "technical failures" without elaborating.
"We have listened to the recordings of the pilot," Transport Minister Elsa Carrera de Escalante said in a radio interview. "It seems there was a blockage in the computer system."
She quoted from a transcript of a message by the pilot, Eric Schreiber, to Lima air traffic control.
Schreiber's final words, according to Carrera, were: "I am reducing engine power, but the plane is still accelerating."
President Alberto Fujimori said the jet was brand new. "The plane ... had three months of flying, that is to say it had all the guarantees, plus an experienced pilot," he told reporters.
Fujimori, who flew over the crash site on Wednesday night, said that rescue efforts would continue through the night.

The Peruvian navy said one of its search planes discovered the wreckage of the airliner soon after 9 a.m. local time (1400 GMT). Adm. Cesar Chavez told reporters a white fuselage, split in two, was spotted floating on the sea about 40 miles (60 km) west of the coastline.
"We have not found any survivors," he said.

At a news conference, Aeroperu officials listed 30 victims from Chile, 20 from Peru, including the nine-man crew, six from Mexico, four from the United States, two from Italy, two from Great Britain, two from Ecuador, and one each from New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.
By early evening, nine bodies had been plucked from the sea and were being transported to Lima for identification.
Hopes of finding survivors dwindled soon after daybreak when helicopters combing the sea reported nothing but oil stains and objects near the coast that looked like baggage.

Officials of Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board, were due to arrive in Lima from the United States early on Thursday and head immediately to the crash site to assist Peruvian investigators.
Boeing officials in Lima declined comment on the cause of the crash.

The jet left Lima at 12.32 a.m. local time (0532 GMT) en route to the Chilean capital of Santiago, according to Aeroperu. It reported technical problems and lost contact at 1.10 a.m. (0610 a.m. GMT) before apparently trying to return to Lima and then crashing off Pasamayo, 55 miles (87 km) north of the capital.

The crash, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local airline Faucett crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
Dense pre-dawn fog initially held up the search and rescue operation.
Fishermen at sea when the plane crashed said they saw a flash of light and heard a dull impact. "We saw the light, but we did not regard it as very important," said one fisherman.
Aeroperu, privatised in 1993 and owned by Aeromexico, said it was operating flights normally on Wednesday morning.

The crash was the third involving a 757, which had a perfect safety record from the time it entered commercial service in 1983 until last year, when an American Airlines jet slammed into a mountain in Colombia, killing 159 people.
In February, a 757-200 crashed into the Caribbean shortly after taking off from the Dominican Republic, killing all 189 people aboard. Both crashes were blamed on pilot error.
